items.claim: Concatenating user input into an argument vector without invoking a shell is not command injection, because the process never parses the argument as shell syntax; the finding only becomes real at the point a shell interpreter is explicitly engaged.
items.disproof: It IS injection when a shell is invoked explicitly with a single composed string, or when the runtime spawns a shell regardless of the call shape (batch files on Windows being the documented case); it is NOT injection when the value stays a discrete argv element in a call that does not implicitly choose a shell, because metacharacters in an unparsed argument have no meaning.

sources.quote: Unlike some other popen functions, this library will not implicitly choose to call a system shell. This means that all characters, including shell metacharacters, can safely be passed to child processes.
The child_process.execFile() function is similar to child_process.exec() except that it does not spawn a shell by default.

items.body: Mechanism: Concatenating user input into an argument vector without invoking a shell is not command injection, because the process never parses the argument as shell syntax; the finding only becomes real at the point a shell interpreter is explicitly engaged. How to apply it in the field: treat this as the fp_rule it is — a hunter must be able to state the concrete observation that demonstrates it, with a request and response in hand, before the finding is reportable. Boundary of the rule: It IS injection when a shell is invoked explicitly with a single composed string, or when the runtime spawns a shell regardless of the call shape (batch files on Windows being the documented case); it is NOT injection when the value stays a discrete argv element in a call that does not implicitly choose a shell, because metacharacters in an unparsed argument have no meaning.

items.claim: The convincing command-injection evidence is a request/response pair where an injected unique marker string comes back verbatim in the command output or in an out-of-band callback, which separates real execution from a blocked or merely reflected payload.
items.disproof: If the marker never appears anywhere the attacker can observe, there is no proof of execution and the report must stay at attempted-injection; a delay or an error message that echoes the payload back does not demonstrate that a process ran, because the echo alone is explained by reflection into the response.

sources.quote: If the shell option is enabled, do not pass unsanitized user input to this function. Any input containing shell metacharacters may be used to trigger arbitrary command execution.

If the shell is invoked explicitly, via shell=True , it is the application’s responsibility to ensure that all whitespace and metacharacters are quoted appropriately to avoid shell injection vulnerabilities.

items.claim: Applying a whole-command metacharacter escaper and calling the argument safe is the classic false negative, because that function is meant for sanitising a command string rather than for quoting a single argument, and the two goals fail in opposite directions.
items.disproof: It IS adequate when every attacker-controlled value is passed as a quoted single argument to a function that treats the quote as a boundary; it is NOT adequate when the value is concatenated into a command string and escaped with the command-level routine, because escaping designed for one position does not establish quoting at an argument boundary and can leave separators live.

sources.quote: This function should be used to escape individual arguments to shell functions coming from user input. The shell functions include exec() , system() and the backtick operator .
On some platforms , it is possible to use shlex.quote() for this escaping.

items.claim: The concrete control that defeats command injection is the absence of a shell at the exec boundary, and the bypass is any code path that turns a safe argv-style call into a shell-invoking one, whether by enabling the shell option, using a legacy shell-invoking helper, or launching a Windows batch file.
items.disproof: It is not a bypass if every reachable path uses the non-shell form and the platform is one where batch-file launching does not implicitly engage a shell; it is a bypass when a single reachable configuration change or a file-type dispatch routes the same user input through a shell, since then the argv boundary that made the call safe no longer exists.

sources.quote: On Windows, batch files ( *.bat or *.cmd ) may be launched by the operating system in a system shell regardless of the arguments passed to this library.
On Windows, however, .bat and .cmd files are not executable on their own without a terminal, and therefore cannot be launched using child_process.execFile() .

items.claim: A 4xx response to an injected payload is not a defence, because many shells still execute the injected portion and the process status is then swallowed by the application, so a non-2xx proves nothing about whether the injected command ran.
items.disproof: It is a genuine defence only when the payload never reached a shell, shown by an out-of-band absence of any effect including no DNS or callback attempt; a clean error page with no side-channel observation is inconclusive rather than exculpatory, and should be recorded as an untested negative.

sources.quote: These operations implicitly invoke the system shell and none of the guarantees described above regarding security and exception handling consistency are valid for these functions.

escapeshellarg() adds single quotes around a string and quotes/escapes any existing single quotes allowing you to pass a string directly to a shell function and having it be treated as a single safe argument.
